content: The Roundabout (Robo) family of proteins consists of single-pass transmembrane receptors that are evolutionarily conserved across a wide range of species, from C. elegans to humans. These proteins were initially identified in Drosophila through a genetic screen aimed at discovering genes involved in axon guidance. The name roundabout was derived from the mutant phenotype observed in Drosophila, where axons exhibited a circular pattern resembling a traffic roundabout. Robo receptors are primarily recognized for their critical role in nervous system development, particularly in responding to secreted Slit ligands. One of the most well-characterized functions of Slit-Robo signaling is its regulation of axonal midline crossing. This signaling pathway is also essential for other neurodevelopmental processes, such as the formation of the olfactory tract, optic nerve, and motor axon fasciculation. Beyond the nervous system, Slit-Robo signaling influences cell migration and the development of various tissues, including the lung, kidney, liver, muscle, and breast. Mutations in Robo genes have been implicated in several neurodevelopmental disorders in humans. The discovery of the Robo family began with a large-scale genetic screen in Drosophila that identified mutants with axon guidance defects. In Robo mutants, axons were observed to cross and recross the midline inappropriately. Subsequent research revealed that the secreted protein Slit serves as the ligand for the Robo receptor. Vertebrate Slit proteins were later identified and shown to bind both vertebrate and Drosophila Robo receptors, mediating axonal repulsion in spinal cord explants. Functional analyses of vertebrate Slit and Robo mutants demonstrated that Slit-Robo signaling regulates commissural axon guidance in vertebrates as well. In vertebrates, Robo1 and Robo2 mediate repulsion in response to Slit, preventing inappropriate midline crossing. However, Robo3 (also known as Rig1) was found to have a unique function: it promotes midline crossing, in contrast to the repulsive roles of Robo1 and Robo2. Phylogenetic studies indicate that all Robo receptors evolved from a common ancestral protein, with subsequent diversification occurring independently in different evolutionary lineages. The Robo gene was first identified in Drosophila and has since been cloned in various species, including mice and humans. Drosophila possesses three Robo receptors: Robo1, Robo2, and Robo3. In vertebrates, four Robo receptors have been identified: Robo1, Robo2, Robo3/Rig1, and Robo4 (also known as Magic Roundabout). In humans, the Robo1 and Robo2 genes are located on chromosome 3p12.3, while Robo3 and Robo4 are found on chromosome 11p24.2. In mice, Robo1 and Robo2 are located on chromosome 16, and Robo3 and Robo4 are on chromosome 9. Alternative splicing of Robo genes generates multiple isoforms with distinct functions. For example, Robo1 undergoes complex splicing to produce variants such as DUTT1, which has been identified as a tumor suppressor gene. Similarly, Robo3/Rig1 is alternatively spliced to produce isoforms with opposing activities during commissural axon guidance. The expression of Robo genes varies across tissues. In humans, Robo1 is broadly expressed throughout the central nervous system. Robo2 is highly expressed in most regions of the adult and fetal brain, as well as in the adult ovary. Intermediate levels of Robo2 expression are observed in the fetal liver and adult lung, kidney, spleen, testes, and spinal cord. Robo3/Rig1 is predominantly expressed in the hindbrain and spinal cord. Robo4 is found in the heart, liver, lungs, kidney, muscle, small intestine, endothelial cells, and placenta. Structurally, Robo proteins share a conserved architecture, including five immunoglobulin-like (Ig) domains, three fibronectin type III (FN3) repeats, a transmembrane domain, and a cytoplasmic domain containing up to four conserved motifs (CC0-3). The Ig1 and Ig2 domains are critical for Slit binding and are conserved across all Robo receptors except for vertebrate Robo4, which has a unique structure with only two Ig and FN3 domains. Despite this structural difference, recent studies suggest that vertebrate Slit2 can bind to Robo4. Robo proteins play a pivotal role in axonal guidance during nervous system development. In bilaterian animals, including insects and mammals, most axons cross the midline during development. In contrast, Robo3 promotes midline crossing by antagonizing the repulsive effects of Robo1 and Robo2. Robo receptors also regulate other axon pathfinding decisions, such as the projection of axons in the optic tract and olfactory epithelium. Beyond the nervous system, Robo proteins guide the migration of non-neural cells, including neuronal precursors, muscle cells, tracheal cells, Langerhans cells, and vascular smooth muscle cells. Robo1 has been implicated in inhibiting glioma invasion and migration. Glioblastoma cells tend to avoid areas with high concentrations of Slit2 and Robo1, suggesting that the Slit2/Robo1 complex acts as a chemorepellent for glioma cells. The binding of Slit to Robo receptors triggers reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, which is mediated by adaptor proteins that interact with the cytoplasmic motifs of Robo receptors. In Drosophila, downstream signaling proteins such as Enabled, Son of Sevenless (SOS), Rac, and Dock have been identified. Activation of Robo1 by Slit leads to actin depolymerization, resulting in growth cone collapse. The signaling mechanisms of Robo2 and Robo3 remain less well understood but are thought to involve distinct pathways. Robo3/Rig1, a more distant member of the Robo family, has a unique role in promoting midline crossing by inhibiting Robo1/2-mediated repulsion. The exact mechanism by which Robo3 achieves this anti-repulsive effect is not fully understood. Robo proteins have clinical relevance in various contexts. Robo4 has been linked to angiogenesis in mice, zebrafish, and human endothelial cells. Robo1 has been associated with both tumor growth and suppression. The Slit2/Robo1 pathway has been implicated in tumor angiogenesis, but Slit2 expression may also suppress tumor growth in certain cancers, such as small cell lung cancer and breast cancer. Robo1 has been linked to dyslexia, potentially through chromosomal translocation, although its role in this condition remains poorly understood. Robo2 has been implicated in developmental disorders such as psychopathy, based on genome-wide linkage studies. Mutations in Robo3/Rig1 cause horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis (HGPPS), a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by impaired horizontal eye movement and progressive spinal curvature. In HGPPS, the absence of Robo3/Rig1 prevents axons in the corticospinal tract and trochlear nerve from crossing the midline, leading to the characteristic symptoms of the disorder.
